problems.description: Moving init_db() to module level makes importing app.py have a side effect (creates the DB file at import time using the default DATABASE path), which runs before the test fixture's monkeypatch takes effect and before any config/env setup.
init_db() is now called both at module import and again inside the test fixture, so the fixture's explicit re-init is partially redundant with the import-time call it cannot avoid.

The mechanical convention score (0.77, 7 violations) is dominated by files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, repositories.py, conftest.py); those violations predate this commit and are not attributable to it.

Static analysis flags 'Classes should use PascalCase' / 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' in the new test_app.py, but the diff contains no classes or module-level constants — these appear to be analyzer false positives, a discrepancy with the qualitative read.

strengths: Comprehensive CRUD coverage (create/list/get/update) asserting real behavior — status codes 201/400/404/200, desc ordering, blank-title validation — not just endpoint existence.
Clean pytest fixture isolating the DB via tmp_path + monkeypatch, so tests never touch the real database.
Moving init_db() out of the __main__ block makes the app deployable under WSGI servers (gunicorn/uwsgi), which never execute the __main__ guard.
Tests verify the 400-on-invalid-input contract that the module-level init now makes reliable under test.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid greenfield session-1 commit that adds a proper isolated test suite and moves DB init out of the __main__ guard (enabling WSGI deployment), with only a minor import-time side-effect concern and a convention score dragged down by pre-existing violations in untouched files.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (hmac/hashlib) instead of an established library; signature is verified with fixed HS256 and compare_digest, but a bespoke token implementation is a known liability source and harder to audit than PyJWT/itsdangerous.
SECRET_KEY falls back to the hardcoded 'dev-secret-key' when env is unset, which would make tokens forgeable if a deployment forgets to set it.

The auth feature (register/login, token_required, owner scoping) lands without accompanying test additions in this commit; the measured convention violations in test_app.py are pre-existing, but no new coverage exercises the added paths.
PRAGMA table_info + ALTER migration runs on every init_db() call; it is guarded and idempotent (only ALTERs once) but adds startup overhead and duplicated schema logic.

strengths: Owner scoping is threaded through every data-access path (get_task, get_tasks, update_task all filter by owner_id), preventing cross-user access — a coherent cross-cutting change applied at the data layer.

Faithfully mirrors existing conventions: section-header comments (# ── Auth routes ──), `with get_db() as conn` context, dict-returning model functions, `dict | None` type hints, and the pre-existing f-string SET-building in update_task.
Uses werkzeug's generate_password_hash instead of storing plaintext passwords.
Migration handles pre-existing tasks tables via a guarded PRAGMA check, keeping the seed codebase forward-compatible.
Dependency-free auth (stdlib + werkzeug only) preserves the minimal-footprint single-file design.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent feature addition that extends the single-file Flask seed with JWT auth and per-user task isolation while faithfully matching existing patterns, though it ships hand-rolled crypto, a dev-secret-key fallback, and no new tests.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay(...) is called synchronously in edit_task with no try/except; if the Redis/Celery broker is unavailable the task-update request 500s, coupling notification-infra availability to the core API path.
BROKER_URL/RESULT_BACKEND are hardcoded to redis://localhost:6379/0 in celery_config.py rather than env-configurable; only the mock/test path makes this safe.
Notification trigger logic (transition-to-completed detection + dispatch) lives in the edit_task view handler instead of a service/domain layer, mixing HTTP and business rules.
Email is synthesized as f'{username}@example.com' and persisted as a real column — a placeholder that silently produces non-deliverable addresses in a real deployment.

Static analysis flags 7 PascalCase/UPPER_CASE violations, but these appear to be heuristic false positives (Celery/MagicMock instantiations) and pre-existing (repositories.py is untouched by this diff), not introduced here.

strengths: Strong test coverage: 7 tests for trigger, non-trigger (title/status changes), idempotence of repeated 'completed' (called once), per-owner email, task-local execution, and broker/routes config.
Follows existing patterns well: get_user_by_id mirrors get_user_by_username, the email ALTER TABLE mirrors the existing owner_id migration in init_db, and token_required/db helpers are reused.
Clean separation of Celery config and tasks into celery_config.py, with an autouse conftest fixture preventing real broker calls during tests.
Idempotent notification (transition-edge detection) is a thoughtful behavioral detail beyond the minimal requirement.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped and thoroughly tested Celery integration that respects existing Flask/db/migration patterns (better), though the synchronous, unguarded .delay() call, hardcoded broker URL, and synthetic email add mild technical debt, and the measured 0.77 convention score appears skewed by heuristic false positives and pre-existing files.

problems.description: Repositories are instantiated as module-level singletons at import time (repositories.py wired to app.py:67-68), coupling them to Flask's g-based get_db before app context exists; fine in practice but makes injection/testability less explicit than constructor wiring in a factory.

BaseRepository builds SQL via f-string interpolation of table_name (repositories.py). Safe today because table_name is a class constant, but the pattern invites unsafe substitution if ever driven by dynamic input; a parameterized table lookup would be safer.

Base class exposes generic get_by_id/get_all/update while concrete repos add owner-scoped variants (get_for_owner/update_for_owner), creating two overlapping access vocabularies; a consistency pass on the base contract would tidy it.

Of the 7 convention violations, most (celery_config.py, conftest.py, test_app.py) are pre-existing and untouched by this diff; only the new repositories.py adds ~1-2 violations (Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE), so the 0.77 score overstates this commit's contribution.

strengths: Clean extraction of the data-access layer: route handlers no longer touch raw SQL, improving separation of concerns in app.py.
Abstract BaseRepository centralizes shared CRUD (get_by_id, get_all, update), removing ~103 lines of duplicated SQLite plumbing.
Connection-factory injection makes repositories testable with a fake DB connection.
Owner-scoped queries (get_for_owner/update_for_owner) preserve the authorization boundary in the DAL instead of relying on call sites.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, convention-following Repository-pattern refactor that removes raw SQL from route handlers and cuts duplication, with only minor concerns around module-level singletons and f-string table names.

compounding_issues: Session 2 hand-rolled JWT (HMAC/base64) instead of using PyJWT, and kept the insecure default SECRET_KEY='dev-secret-key' through all 5 sessions — security-sensitive crypto never upgraded.

Session 4's BaseRepository.get_all()/get_by_id()/update()/delete() are owner-unscoped on TaskRepository; routes only use the scoped variants, so no current bug, but a latent cross-user data-leak path remains for any future caller.

Session 5 silently broke the GET /tasks contract: response shape changed from an array to {data, next_cursor, total} and ordering flipped DESC→ASC (needed for stable cursor pagination) — a breaking API change with no versioning.
Ad-hoc PRAGMA-based ALTER TABLE migrations stack up in init_db() each session (owner_id in S2, email in S3) — works, but there is no proper migration system and it grows fragile.
Celery broker/backend URI and rate-limit storage are hardcoded to redis://localhost:6379/0 in celery_config.py (only the rate-limit URI is env-configurable) — fine only because tests mock the broker.
key_decisions: Session 1: moving init_db() to module import time and building the tmp_path/monkeypatch test fixture — established the testability foundation every later session built on.

Session 2: adding JWT auth with per-user task isolation (owner_id column + scoped queries) — the pivotal architectural decision; the owner-scoping invariant is preserved through every later layer (repository, pagination, rate-limit keying).
Session 3: integrating Celery + Redis for async completion notifications with an autouse mock fixture so tests never touch the broker — async added without breaking the test harness.
Session 4: extracting a Repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository) that moved all SQL out of routes — the refactor that made session 5's pagination addition clean.
Session 5: cursor-based pagination with per-user flask-limiter rate limiting (keyed on verified user id, falling back to remote address) — productionization as the capstone.
Consistent test-first discipline: test suite grew with every feature (85→164→232+ test lines), all external deps mocked, final state at 0.823 test/code ratio.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved. Session 1 established a solid test harness and moved DB init to import time; session 2 delivered the largest feature (auth + per-user isolation) with comprehensive tests and a schema migration; session 3 cleanly integrated async Celery notifications behind mocks; session 4 was a pure refactor that shrank app.py by ~120 lines and isolated all SQL behind a repository layer (code lines fell while structure improved); session 5 added rate limiting and cursor pagination, updating all affected tests. Every session left the suite green (39 tests pass at HEAD, all_successful=true), with the only cost being a deliberate, unversioned breaking change to the list endpoint's response contract.
story_review.summary: A textbook-compoundable story: each session's decision (testability, owner-scoping, async integration, repository extraction) made the next session easier rather than harder, ending on a production-quality API with rate limiting and pagination — the strongest progression shape.
